marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q015.takeaway: Pterion is a thin H-shaped junction over the anterior middle meningeal artery.
marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q015.displayText: An extradural hematoma at the pterion is a result of injury to the anterior division of the middle meningeal artery. The pterion is an H-shaped sutural junction between the frontal bone, squamous temporal bone, greater wing of sphenoid and parietal bone. It also overlies the lateral fissure of the cerebral hemisphere, so the hematoma can cause compressive lesions.
emphasis: anterior division of the middle meningeal artery

rationales.a: Superficial temporal artery is a terminal external-carotid branch and is not the vessel vulnerable beneath pterion.
rationales.b: Maxillary artery gives rise to middle meningeal artery; it is not itself the vessel typically torn at pterion.
rationales.d: Deep temporal arteries supply temporalis, not the epidural vessel at pterion.

marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q016.takeaway: Anterior fontanelle is last to close and may remain open at 18 months.
marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q016.displayText: The anterior fontanelle is most likely to be open because it is the last fontanelle to close. It closes at around 18-24 months of age. The source provides a table of fontanelles, their locations and closure times.

rationales.b: Posterior fontanelle closes within the first few months, much earlier than 18 months.
rationales.c: Occipital fontanelle also closes early in infancy, not as late as the anterior fontanelle.
rationales.d: Mastoid fontanelle usually closes in infancy and is not the latest fontanelle.

marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q017.takeaway: Arcuate eminence overlies the superior semicircular canal.
marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q017.displayText: The superior semicircular canal is present beneath the arcuate eminence of the petrous temporal bone. The arcuate eminence is used as a neurosurgical landmark for the superior semicircular canal in surgeries done by the middle cranial fossa approach. The temporal bone consists of squamous, mastoid, petrous and tympanic parts, as well as the styloid and zygomatic processes. The petrous temporal bone is a pyramid-shaped structure. Its relations include: inferior to the arcuate eminence - superior semicircular canal; posterior surface - internal auditory meatus and vestibular aqueduct; inferior surface - carotid canal and jugular fossa (jugular notch).

rationales.a: Lesser petrosal nerve passes through skull-base foramina/canals and is not the bony structure under arcuate eminence.
rationales.b: Greater petrosal nerve traverses petrous temporal bone but does not lie immediately beneath arcuate eminence.
rationales.d: Posterior semicircular canal is not the canal directly beneath arcuate eminence; the source identifies superior canal.

marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q018.takeaway: Temporal bone zygomatic process joins zygomatic bone to form zygomatic arch.
marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q018.displayText: The X-ray shows a fracture of the left zygomatic arch. The zygomatic process of the temporal bone contributes to formation of the zygomatic arch. The zygomatic arch is made up of the temporal process of the zygomatic bone and the zygomatic process of the temporal bone; they articulate at the zygomaticotemporal suture. The masseter originates from the lower border of the zygomatic arch.
emphasis: zygomatic process of the temporal bone

rationales.a: Frontal bone does not contribute a process to zygomatic arch.
rationales.b: Maxilla supports the facial skeleton but is not one of the two bones that form the arch.
rationales.c: Sphenoid forms part of orbit/skull base but does not supply the zygomatic process forming the arch.

marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q019.takeaway: Lesser occipital nerve supplies scalp posterior to ear and vertex.
marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q019.displayText: The lesser occipital nerve provides sensory innervation to the scalp. Anterior to the ear and vertex, sensory supply is by branches of the trigeminal nerve; posterior to the ear and vertex, sensory supply is by spinal nerves. The temporal and posterior auricular branches of the facial nerve constitute the motor supply to the anterior and posterior scalp, respectively.
emphasis: posterior to the ear and vertex

rationales.a: Infraorbital nerve supplies midface, not scalp behind ear and vertex.
rationales.c: Greater auricular nerve supplies lower auricle and skin over parotid/angle of mandible, not the posterior scalp region asked.
rationales.d: Facial nerve branches provide motor supply to scalp muscles, not its cutaneous sensory supply.

marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q020.takeaway: Subaponeurotic loose areolar tissue communicates with intracranial venous channels through emissary veins.
marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q020.displayText: The infection has likely spread from the sub-aponeurotic tissue. The sub-aponeurotic loose areolar tissue of the scalp is referred to as the dangerous area of the scalp. Infection from this layer can pass into the cranial cavity through small emissary veins, which pass through parietal foramina in the calvaria. It can reach intracranial structures causing meningitis and intracranial abscesses. The scalp consists of 5 layers (mnemonic - SCALP): skin; connective tissue; aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica) with occipitofrontalis muscle; loose areolar (sub-aponeurotic) tissue; and pericranium.

rationales.a: Superficial fascia is not the loose subaponeurotic plane that communicates through emissary veins.
rationales.b: Galea aponeurotica is the dense tendon layer, not the dangerous loose plane.
rationales.d: Pericranium covers skull; the emissary-vein route from scalp abscess is through subaponeurotic tissue.

marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q021.takeaway: Dense connective tissue fixes scalp arteries open, causing profuse arterial bleeding.
marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q021.displayText: Scalp bleeding is predominantly arterial, from the dense connective tissue of the scalp. Profuse bleeding from scalp injuries occurs because of low venous pressure in the erect posture and because the dense connective tissue holds the arteries open and does not allow them to retract, causing profuse bleeding. The scalp has an extremely rich blood supply from branches of the external carotid arteries. Profuse bleeding from a scalp laceration requires rapid control by sutures.

rationales.a: Venous bleeding/loose areolar tissue does not explain the profuse arterial bleed held open by dense connective tissue.
rationales.b: Dense connective tissue is correct layer, but scalp vessels are predominantly arterial rather than venous.
rationales.d: Arterial bleeding is correct, but loose areolar tissue is not the layer binding arteries open.

marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q022.takeaway: Levator palpebrae superioris is supplied by CN III/sympathetics, not facial nerve.
marrow__ANAT_CH28_Q022.displayText: The motor component of levator palpebrae superioris is innervated by the oculomotor (III cranial) nerve and the smooth muscle component is innervated by sympathetic nerves. It is uninvolved in Bell's palsy. All the other listed facial muscles are innervated by the facial nerve and therefore can be paralyzed in Bell's palsy.

rationales.a: Orbicularis oris is facial-nerve supplied and can be affected in Bell palsy.
rationales.b: Frontalis is supplied by temporal branch of facial nerve.
rationales.c: Orbicularis oculi is supplied by facial nerve and can be weak in Bell palsy; levator palpebrae is the exception.
